{{Short description|Finite topological space with two points, only one of which is closed}}
{{distinguish|Sierpiński set}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Sierpiński space''' is a [[finite topological space]] with two points, only one of which is [[closed set|closed]].<ref>{{nlab|id=Sierpinski+space |title=Sierpinski space}}</ref>
It is the smallest example of a [[topological space]] which is neither [[trivial topology|trivial]] nor [[discrete topology|discrete]]. It is named after [[Wacław Sierpiński]].

The Sierpiński space has important relations to the [[Computability theory|theory of computation]] and [[semantics]],<ref>An online paper, it explains the motivation, why the notion of “topology” can be applied in the investigation of concepts of the computer science. Alex Simpson: [https://web.archive.org/web/20160918181508/http://homepages.inf.ed.ac.uk/als/Teaching/MSfS Mathematical Structures for Semantics] [http://www.dcs.ed.ac.uk/home/als/Teaching/MSfS/ (original)]. Chapter III: [https://web.archive.org/web/20160918181508/http://homepages.inf.ed.ac.uk/als/Teaching/MSfS/l3.ps Topological Spaces from a Computational Perspective] [http://www.dcs.ed.ac.uk/home/als/Teaching/MSfS/l3.ps (original)]. The “References” section provides many online materials on [[domain theory]].</ref><ref>{{cite book | title = Synthetic topology of data types and classical spaces | last1 = Escardó | first1 = Martín | publisher = [[Elsevier]] | year = 2004 | series = Electronic Notes in Theoretical Computer Science | volume = 87 | page = 2004 | citeseerx = 10.1.1.129.2886 }}</ref> because it is the [[classifying space]] for [[open sets]] in the [[Scott topology]].

==Definition and fundamental properties==

Explicitly, the Sierpiński space is a [[topological space]] ''S''  whose underlying [[set (mathematics)|point set]] is <math>\{0, 1\}</math> and whose [[open set]]s are
<math display=block>\{\varnothing,\{1\}, \{0,1\}\}.</math>
The [[closed set]]s are
<math display=block>\{\varnothing, \{0\}, \{0,1\}\}.</math>
So the [[singleton set]] <math>\{0\}</math> is closed and the set <math>\{1\}</math> is open (<math>\varnothing = \{ \, \}</math> is the [[empty set]]).

The [[Kuratowski closure axioms|closure operator]] on ''S'' is determined by
<math display=block>\overline{\{0\}} = \{0\}, \qquad \overline{\{1\}} = \{0,1\}.</math>

A finite topological space is also uniquely determined by its [[specialization preorder]]. For  the Sierpiński space this [[preorder]] is actually a [[total order]] and given by
<math display=block>0 \leq 0, \qquad 0 \leq 1, \qquad 1 \leq 1.</math>

==Topological properties==

The Sierpiński space <math>S</math> is a special case of both the finite [[particular point topology]] (with particular point 1) and the finite [[excluded point topology]] (with excluded point 0). Therefore, <math>S</math> has many properties in common with one or both of these families.

===Separation===

*The points 0 and 1 are [[topologically distinguishable]] in ''S'' since <math>\{1\}</math> is an open set which contains only one of these points. Therefore, ''S'' is a [[Kolmogorov space|Kolmogorov (T<sub>0</sub>) space]].
*However, ''S'' is not [[T1 space|T<sub>1</sub>]] since the point 1 is not closed. It follows that ''S'' is not [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]], or T<sub>''n''</sub> for any <math>n \geq 1.</math>
*''S'' is not [[regular space|regular]] (or [[completely regular]]) since the point 1 and the disjoint closed set <math>\{0\}</math> cannot be [[separated set|separated by neighborhoods]]. (Also regularity in the presence of T<sub>0</sub> would imply Hausdorff.)
*''S'' is [[vacuous truth|vacuously]] [[normal space|normal]] and [[completely normal space|completely normal]] since there are no nonempty [[separated set]]s.
*''S'' is not [[perfectly normal space|perfectly normal]] since the disjoint closed sets <math>\varnothing</math> and <math>\{0\}</math> cannot be precisely separated by a function. Indeed, <math>\{0\}</math> cannot be the [[zero set]] of any [[continuous function (topology)|continuous function]] <math>S \to \Reals</math> since every such function is [[constant function|constant]].

===Connectedness===

*The Sierpiński space ''S'' is both [[hyperconnected]] (since every nonempty open set contains 1) and [[ultraconnected]] (since every nonempty closed set contains 0).
*It follows that ''S'' is both [[connected space|connected]] and [[path connected space|path connected]]. 
*A [[path (topology)|path]] from 0 to 1 in ''S'' is given by the function: <math>f(0) = 0</math> and <math>f(t) = 1</math> for <math>t > 0.</math> The function <math>f : I \to S</math> is continuous since <math>f^{-1}(1) = (0, 1]</math> which is open in ''I''.
*Like all finite topological spaces, ''S'' is [[locally path connected]].
*The Sierpiński space is [[contractible space|contractible]], so the [[fundamental group]] of ''S'' is [[trivial group|trivial]] (as are all the [[higher homotopy groups]]).

===Compactness===

*Like all finite topological spaces, the Sierpiński space is both [[compact space|compact]] and [[second-countable]].
*The compact subset <math>\{1\}</math> of ''S'' is not closed showing that compact subsets of T<sub>0</sub> spaces need not be closed.
*Every [[open cover]] of ''S'' must contain ''S'' itself since ''S'' is the only open neighborhood of 0. Therefore, every open cover of ''S'' has an open [[subcover]] consisting of a single set: <math>\{S\}.</math>
*It follows that ''S'' is [[fully normal space|fully normal]].<ref>Steen and Seebach incorrectly list the Sierpiński space as {{em|not}} being fully normal (or fully T<sub>4</sub> in their terminology).</ref>

===Convergence===

*Every [[sequence]] in ''S'' [[limit of a sequence|converges]] to the point 0. This is because the only neighborhood of 0 is ''S'' itself.
*A sequence in ''S'' converges to 1 if and only if the sequence contains only finitely many terms equal to 0 (i.e. the sequence is eventually just 1's).
*The point 1 is a [[cluster point]] of a sequence in ''S'' if and only if the sequence contains infinitely many 1's.
*''Examples'':
**1 is not a cluster point of <math>(0,0,0,0,\ldots).</math>
**1 is a cluster point (but not a limit) of <math>(0,1,0,1,0,1,\ldots).</math>
**The sequence <math>(1,1,1,1,\ldots)</math> converges to both 0 and 1.

===Metrizability===

*The Sierpiński space ''S'' is not [[metrizable space|metrizable]] or even [[pseudometrizable space|pseudometrizable]] since every pseudometric space is [[Tychonoff space|completely regular]] but the Sierpiński space is not even [[Regular space|regular]].
* ''S'' is generated by the [[hemimetric]] (or [[pseudometric space|pseudo]]-[[quasimetric]]) <math>d(0, 1) = 0</math> and <math>d(1,0) = 1.</math>

===Other properties===

*There are only three [[continuous function (topology)|continuous maps]] from ''S'' to itself: the [[identity function|identity map]] and the [[constant map]]s to 0 and 1.
*It follows that the [[homeomorphism group]] of ''S'' is [[trivial group|trivial]].

==Continuous functions to the Sierpiński space==

Let ''X'' be an arbitrary set. The [[function space|set of all functions]] from ''X'' to the set <math>\{0, 1\}</math> is typically denoted <math>2^X.</math> These functions are precisely the [[indicator function|characteristic function]]s of ''X''. Each such function is of the form
<math display=block>\chi_U(x) = \begin{cases}1 & x \in U \\ 0 & x \not\in U\end{cases}</math>
where ''U'' is a [[subset]] of ''X''. In other words, the set of functions <math>2^X</math> is in [[bijective]] correspondence with <math>P(X),</math> the [[power set]] of ''X''. Every subset ''U'' of ''X'' has its characteristic function <math>\chi_U</math> and every function from ''X'' to <math>\{0, 1\}</math> is of this form.

Now suppose ''X'' is a topological space and let <math>\{0, 1\}</math> have the Sierpiński topology. Then a function <math>\chi_U : X \to S</math> is [[Continuous function (topology)|continuous]] if and only if <math>\chi_U^{-1}(1)</math> is open in ''X''. But, by definition
<math display=block>\chi_U^{-1}(1) = U.</math>
So <math>\chi_U</math> is continuous if and only if ''U'' is open in ''X''. Let <math>C(X, S)</math> denote the set of all continuous maps from ''X'' to ''S'' and let <math>T(X)</math> denote the topology of ''X'' (that is, the family of all open sets). Then we have a bijection from  <math>T(X)</math> to <math>C(X, S)</math> which sends the open set <math>U</math> to <math>\chi_U.</math>
<math display=block>C(X, S) \cong T(X)</math>
That is, if we identify <math>2^X</math> with <math>P(X)</math> the subset of continuous maps <math>C(X, S) \subseteq 2^X</math> is precisely the topology of <math>X:</math> <math>T(X) \subseteq P(X).</math>

A particularly notable example of this is the [[Scott topology]] for [[partially ordered set]]s, in which the Sierpiński space becomes the [[classifying space]] for open sets when the characteristic function preserves [[directed join]]s.<ref>{{nlab|id=Scott+topology|title=Scott topology}}</ref>

===Categorical description===

The above construction can be described nicely using the language of [[category theory]]. There is a [[contravariant functor]] <math>T : \mathbf{Top} \to \mathbf{Set}</math> from the [[category of topological spaces]] to the [[category of sets]] which assigns each topological space <math>X</math> its set of open sets <math>T(X)</math> and each continuous function <math>f : X \to Y</math> the [[preimage]] map
<math display=block>f^{-1} : T(Y) \to T(X).</math>
The statement then becomes: the functor <math>T</math> is [[representable functor|represented]] by <math>(S, \{1\})</math> where <math>S</math> is the Sierpiński space. That is, <math>T</math> is [[naturally isomorphic]] to the [[Hom functor]] <math>\operatorname{Hom}(-, S)</math> with the natural isomorphism determined by the [[universal element]] <math>\{1\} \in T(S).</math>  This is generalized by the notion of a [[presheaf (category theory)|presheaf]].<ref>[[Saunders MacLane]], [[Ieke Moerdijk]], ''Sheaves in Geometry and Logic: A First Introduction to Topos Theory'', (1992) Springer-Verlag Universitext {{isbn|978-0387977102}}</ref>

===The initial topology===

Any topological space ''X'' has the [[initial topology]] induced by the family <math>C(X, S)</math> of continuous functions to Sierpiński space. Indeed, in order to [[coarser topology|coarsen]] the topology on ''X'' one must remove open sets. But removing the open set ''U'' would render <math>\chi_U</math> discontinuous. So ''X'' has the coarsest topology for which each function in <math>C(X, S)</math> is continuous.

The family of functions <math>C(X, S)</math> [[separating set|separates points]] in ''X'' if and only if ''X'' is a [[T0 space|T<sub>0</sub> space]]. Two points <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> will be separated by the function <math>\chi_U</math> if and only if the open set ''U'' contains precisely one of the two points. This is exactly what it means for <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> to be [[topologically distinguishable]].

Therefore, if ''X'' is T<sub>0</sub>, we can embed ''X'' as a [[Subspace (topology)|subspace]] of a [[product topology|product]] of Sierpiński spaces, where there is one copy of ''S'' for each open set ''U'' in ''X''. The embedding map
<math display=block>e : X \to \prod_{U \in T(X)} S = S^{T(X)}</math>
is given by
<math display=block>e(x)_U = \chi_U(x).\,</math>
Since subspaces and products of T<sub>0</sub> spaces are T<sub>0</sub>, it follows that a topological space is T<sub>0</sub> if and only if it is [[homeomorphic]] to a subspace of a power of ''S''.

==In algebraic geometry==

In [[algebraic geometry]] the Sierpiński space arises as the [[spectrum of a ring|spectrum]] <math>\operatorname{Spec}(R)</math> of a [[discrete valuation ring]] <math>R</math> such as <math>\Z_{(p)}</math> (the [[localization of a ring|localization]] of the [[integer]]s at the [[prime ideal]] generated by the prime number <math>p</math>). The [[generic point]] of <math>\operatorname{Spec}(R),</math> coming from the [[zero ideal]], corresponds to the open point 1, while the [[special point]] of <math>\operatorname{Spec}(R),</math> coming from the unique [[maximal ideal]], corresponds to the [[closed point]] 0.
